chunks: Voltage mode vs current mode control. The question: What is the difference between voltage-mode and current-mode control? Why are they often both implemented simultaneously?
Voltage mode has one loop: it measures the output voltage and sets the duty cycle. Current mode adds a second, inner loop that watches the inductor current.
The error amplifier sets a current limit for each cycle instead of a duty cycle.
This makes the part being controlled (the plant) behave more simply, so the loop is easier to stabilize, and it protects the switch.
Imagine heating a house with one thermometer in the living room. That is voltage mode: you only act when the room has already cooled.
Now add a sensor on the heater that limits how hard it can run, so you can react right away to a cold draft and never overheat the heater. That is current mode.
The extra sensor also brings a cost: it picks up noise from the switching.
Control-to-output frequency response for the same L , C , ESR and load. The voltage-mode plant (steeper) has the resonance at 10. 7 kilohertz and falls to -180^ degrees .
The current-mode plant has a single pole near 1 kilohertz and its phase stays near -90^ degrees until the ESR zero.
Notice the much easier phase situation for a crossover at, say, 40 kilohertz in CM: about -90^ degrees of lag instead of -180^ degrees .
The sampling double pole at f sw over 2 is not shown.
Voltage mode: one loop; the error voltage is compared to a ramp to set the duty cycle ("Buck control topologies compared").
Current mode: an inner loop on the inductor current plus an outer voltage loop. Peak current: the level at which the switch turns off in peak current mode.
Compensator: the circuit that shapes the loop for stability ("What stability means in a buck").
Slope compensation: an added ramp that prevents instability above 50% duty ("Subharmonic oscillation explained").
A 12 volts to 3. 3 volts buck has D equals 0. 275 . In voltage mode, if the ramp spans 0 to 2 volts, an error voltage of 0. 55 volts gives D equals 0. 55 over 2 equals 0. 275 .
In current mode, the error amplifier instead says, for example, "turn off at 3. 5 amps". The switch turns on at the clock and turns off when the inductor current reaches 3.
5 amps. That is the whole idea.
"Voltage mode has one loop: the error amplifier output is compared to a fixed ramp to set duty, and the plant is the full second-order LC, so it needs type III compensation.
Current mode adds an inner loop on the inductor current: the outer loop sets a current command and the switch turns off when the inductor current reaches it.
The inductor then looks like a current source, so the plant is first-order, compensation is easier, line changes are rejected and you get cycle-by-cycle current limit.
Current mode is both at once: an outer voltage loop for regulation and an inner current loop for fast control and protection."
